input: This case examines the pricing of a SaaS tier. The tier is priced at $59 per unit, against a variable cost of $33 per unit, which leaves a contribution of $26 per unit towards the fixed costs, and the fixed costs amount to $305k per year. On this basis, the break-even volume works out at 11731 units per year, the volume at which the total contribution exactly covers the fixed costs. The current volume, however, is only 6144 units per year, which is 5587 units per year below the break-even level, so at the current volume the tier does not cover its fixed costs and runs below break-even by that margin. Closing the gap would require the volume to rise to 11731 units per year at the current price and cost structure. The structure of the case is a familiar one: each unit sold contributes a fixed amount after its variable cost, and the tier becomes viable only when enough of those contributions have accumulated to meet the fixed costs for the year. It is worth noting that the volume figures used here are last year's actuals, and that the effect of the price on volume has not been estimated. This means that the gap, while clearly quantified on the stated basis, cannot by itself say how the volume would respond if the price were changed, and any pricing decision would need to take that missing relationship into account before treating the break-even figure as a target.
target: At the current volume of 6144 units per year, the SaaS tier runs below its break-even volume of 11731 units per year, a shortfall of 5587 units per year. The price is $59 per unit and the variable cost is $33 per unit, giving a contribution of $26 per unit. Fixed costs are $305k per year, and the break-even volume of 11731 units per year is the volume at which the contribution covers those fixed costs: below it, each year closes with part of the fixed costs uncovered; at it, the tier exactly pays its way. The shortfall is stated in units because the contribution per unit converts it directly into the uncovered share of the fixed costs. Three quantities could close the gap, and the case separates them. Volume could rise at the current price, which is the route the shortfall states. Price could rise, which raises the contribution per unit but acts on a volume whose response to price is unknown. Costs could fall, on either the variable or the fixed side, which lowers the break-even volume directly. The case quantifies the first route and leaves the other two as directions rather than figures, because the numbers it contains fix the break-even volume only for the price and costs as they stand. The volume figures are last year's actuals. The effect of the price on volume is not estimated, so the case states the gap at the current price and cannot state the volume that a different price would bring; a price change argued from this case alone would rest on a relationship the case does not contain.
